facts.fact: Male bettas build bubble nests at the water surface, sometimes anchored to plants or rocks, and often build them even when no female is present.
During spawning the male wraps his body around the female in a 'nuptial embrace', and each embrace releases about 10–40 eggs.
Females can release 12 to 492 eggs in one spawning.
One guide says females can lay about 20 to 500 eggs.
The male picks up sinking eggs in his mouth, places them in the nest, repairs the nest and guards the eggs until they hatch.
Bettas can become sexually mature at 4–5 months.
The labyrinth organ usually develops at three to six weeks of age. Before then, free-swimming fry breathe with their gills.
One spawn can produce hundreds of fry, so plan space and buyers before breeding.
A female ready to spawn darkens and shows vertical 'breeding bars'.
Signs of a gravid female include about five to six lighter, slightly uneven vertical bands and a white egg spot (ovipositor) just behind the ventral fins. Not every female shows the bands.
A gravid female looks rounded mainly at the sides when seen from above. A heavily rounded belly with no bands or egg spot may mean constipation or dropsy instead.
A female can hold her eggs for one to two weeks.
Eggs start out milky white, and fertilized eggs develop dark flecks.
Small white specks in the bubble nest show that the pair has spawned.
A courting male flares his gills, spreads his fins and twists his body in a dance-like display.
Females have an ovipositor tube. Differences between the sexes become visible about two months after hatching.
Choose healthy parents with good form, because the fry inherit their qualities. The Vietnamese guide gives about 8 months as the most fertile breeding age.
One guide recommends breeding fish aged about four to twelve months, with the female the same size as the male or slightly smaller.
Condition both fish for two to four weeks with three or four small meals a day: one of flake or pellets, the rest live or frozen foods.
Conditioning foods include bloodworms, brine shrimp, California blackworms and Daphnia. Live or frozen food works better than prepared food.
Spawning tank: about 10 gallons (39 liters) holding about 4 gallons (15 liters) of water, heated to 80–82°F (27–28°C), with no filter and a lid.
Another guide uses a bare-bottom tank with 5 inches of conditioned water at about 80°F (26.6°C), pH 6.5 and 4–8 dGH, plus a heater, a baffled sponge filter, floating plants and a divider.
Add Java moss, Indian almond leaves and a floating piece of bubble wrap as a nest anchor. A cut 2-liter bottle can hold the female inside the tank.
Vietnamese method: fill a large tank (about 80×30×30 cm) to about 10 cm with salted water, set a small bottomless tank inside it for the female, and keep the male in the large tank.
The Vietnamese guide keeps the pair apart in the two compartments for about 1 week so they get used to each other before meeting.
Put leaves in one corner (almond leaves, water lettuce, lettuce with stems removed, or water hyacinth) so hatchlings rest on them instead of the bottom.
Release the female once the male has built a bubble nest, often after an overnight introduction across a divider.
The male builds a nest in about 12 to 24 hours. The female inspects it and may reject it.
Spawning can last 24 to 36 hours.
Spawning may take up to about 2 days. Do not feed the pair while they spawn.
Remove the female after spawning, or as soon as the male starts chasing her away from the nest.
Eggs incubate for 24–36 hours, and larvae stay in the nest for two to three days until their yolk sacs are used up.
The Vietnamese guide says eggs hatch in about 2 days and fry swim steadily after about 3 days.
Remove the male when the fry become free-swimming, about 2–3 days after hatching. Feed him protein-rich food, since he has probably not eaten for a week or more.
Separate the male and raise the fry on their own once the fry swim horizontally and steadily.
Do not feed fry for the first 24–48 hours while they absorb their yolk sacs.

Fry feeding schedule from one guide: infusoria in week 1; baby brine shrimp from about week 1; finely grated frozen bloodworms at 3–4 weeks; grindal worms or blackworms at 5–6 weeks; finely grated, pre-soaked pellets at 8–9 weeks.
Feed fry 4–5 small meals a day, giving only what they can eat each time.
First fry foods can include egg yolk dissolved in dechlorinated water and dripped in by pipette 2–3 times a day, followed by microworms, vinegar eels and baby brine shrimp.
About a week after the fry become free-swimming, raise the water level and add a gentle sponge filter.
Keep fry in the breeding tank for three to four weeks, then move them to a grow-out tank. They are fully developed at three to four months.
Change 10–20% of the fry tank water often, using treated water.
Separate males before they turn aggressive. Early signs appear at roughly 8–9 weeks, and territorial fighting at 3–6 months. Aggressive females also need separating.
Keep fry water at a steady 78–80°F (25.5–26.7°C), and have a spare heater ready in case one fails.
The Vietnamese guide adds salt to the large tank and tetracycline to the female's compartment before introduction, but gives no doses.
Velvet (Piscinoodinium sp.) is a common killer of betta fry in captivity.
Cover the tank, leaving only a small gap for light, so people passing by do not frighten the pair.
Do not startle the male while he cares for the fry, because he may eat them.
Freeze tubifex and white worms before feeding them, because they can carry parasites.
After spawning, females need at least four weeks of rest before breeding again. Males need about a week.
A female that cannot release her eggs can become egg-bound and risk infection. The guide suggests a proper diet and keeping her near a male.
Dropping the female straight into the male's tank without a divider stage can lead to attacks.
Leaving the female with the male after spawning is a mistake, because the male may kill her or she may eat the eggs.
Overfeeding adults or fry fouls the water.
Strong filter flow can suck fry in. Use a sponge filter on low flow.
Dry pellets that are not soaked can cause bloat or constipation, and pellets should not be fed in the first 6–9 weeks.
Disturbing the eggs can make the male abandon the nest.
Vietnamese breeders use live 'bo bo' (water fleas) as fry food: hold the catch in clean water for a day, remove the dead ones, and scoop the live ones off the surface, avoiding very dark ones.
At about 2 weeks, the Vietnamese guide adds 2 almond leaves (lá bàng) to the large tank and 1 to the small tank to help balance pH, and keeps the water level at about 10 cm.
A betta farm in Hiệp Bình Chánh, Thủ Đức, Ho Chi Minh City started with 150 breeding pairs supplied by the district agricultural extension station in 2015.
On that HCMC farm the main foods are mosquito larvae (lăng quăng) and bo bo, and fry are raised for about 3 months before sale.
Vietnamese breeders pair parents so that colors are balanced and fin and tail proportions are harmonious. One pair gives from a few dozen to several hundred offspring.
In a study on betta fry, survival with ketapang (Terminalia catappa) leaves at 1 g/L, betel (Piper betle) leaves at 1 g/L, or 0.5 g/L of each ranged from 13.33% to 60.00% across treatments.
With good care, about 90% of fry may survive.
Expect to keep roughly 80–90% of fry, with most losses in the first few days.
Newly hatched fry are about 0.76 mm, and they reach about 21.6–33 mm by 9–12 weeks.
Fry show color at about eight weeks.
Bettas do not get 'pregnant'. They lay eggs, and a female carrying eggs is called gravid (Fish Tank Advisor).
Removing a bubble nest during cleaning is not a disaster, because the male will build another (Fish Tank Advisor).
